ITU Copenhagen · Autumn 2026 · Thursdays

Technical Interaction Design / Weekly Syllabus

A fast technical track builds and deploys a working app in the first five weeks. At the same time, a design track focuses on understanding users, designing for them, and improving the design.

  • Every team builds the same basic to-do app, but adds their own feature for a specific group of users.
  • Each week includes a lecture, a two-hour exercise, and a project milestone.
  • Use the basic app yourself, design the new feature for people different from you, and be able to explain all your code at the exam.
  • All work is due Tuesday at midnight.

Before week 1, you only need to complete JavaScript, the Language. The other TopUps are introduced later, just before you need them.

In the AI era, the important skill is understanding code, not just writing it. You can use AI as much as you want, but you must understand and explain every line of code at the exam. The course is designed around this idea.

Each design deliverable lands about two weeks after the lecture that teaches it, leaving nine days to read it — the feedback then opens the next lecture, in weeks 6, 9 and 12. The user study gets a further week after that to act on what the feedback found, before wireframing starts. Checkpoints you hit and dogfood against, not submissions marked line-by-line. Two sit-down conversations per group, in weeks 7 and 10: scope and data model, then mid-project.
Week 01
Aug 27
MirceaLecture · React I + opening
First React app: components, props & state
The course opens with a story: a real app, and the people it was built for. Then straight into React: components, JSX, props, state, event handling, and rendering lists with keys, built live on a tiny to-do app. It ends with an app that works and is obviously silly — Add picks a task at random from a list of samples, because you cannot type one in yet. Next week you can.
Exercise · 2h solo
first hourScaffold your own app with Vite, following the starter kit — npm create, npm install, npm run dev — and look at what appeared: package.json, node_modules, and what “a package” actually is. Strip the boilerplate, rebuild the class to-do from your notes: an array of items, a component with props, keys. Then change one thing. Commit it to week-01/ in a public exercise repo.
second hourKeep playing with what you built — another field, a count of what is left, whatever you want to try. Then go and find your group of four, due Tue 8 Sep.
GH

Week 02
Sep 3
MirceaLecture · React II
React, part two: forms, lists, and local persistence
The week the to-do becomes a real app. The random Add button becomes a form you type into: controlled components. Then conditional rendering; keys and IDs, and why they start to matter the moment things can be removed — last week's list was keyed by index, which is fine until something is deleted from the middle; delete and check-off; then useEffect, and persistence through local storage. It is also the week to stop debugging by console.log: a debugger; statement costs nothing and pauses the moment DevTools is open, VS Code can hold the breakpoint instead, and the React DevTools component tree lets you see state rather than print it — which is what separates “the list did not update” from “the state changed but the key did not”. Conditional rendering is quietly load-bearing — it is how week 4 gates the app on a logged-in user, with no router in sight. Local storage is what makes useEffect earn its place: something outside React has to be kept in step. It also sets week 4 up as a clean swap rather than a new idea — same hook, same shape, Parse instead of the browser.
Exercise · 2h solo
first hourBuild one controlled form from scratch; add delete and check-off with stable IDs.
second hourStill individual — carry it further in your own repo: add, edit, delete and check off items, then persist to local storage.
GH

Week 03
Sep 10
KonstantinaLecture · Design IMircea away
Understanding user needs
Interviews and thematic analysis, pointed at your population: how to ask, how to listen, and how to turn transcripts into themes rather than into the quotes you happened to like. Personas get a mention because you will meet them in industry, but they are not the point here and a persona invented at a desk is worth nothing — whatever you write down has to have come out of the study. Then the step that makes them usable — mapping each theme to a Lauesen-style task, so a finding becomes something the app can do. The thematic-analysis portion is taught by a TA who has done one for their own thesis. The onion: the core is lists + items + sharing; every extra feature must earn its ring or it doesn’t ship.

Week 04
Sep 17
MirceaLecture · Backend I
Replacing local storage with a real database
Parse: the backend, the SDK, and the to-do list you already have, re-implemented on top of it. Two weeks ago the to-do survived a refresh through local storage; now it survives a different browser. The one useEffect that rewrote the whole array cannot survive the trip, and what replaces it — one call per change, behind a service layer — is the shape of every backend app you will write. The data does not arrive instantly any more either, which gives every fetching component three states instead of one. And then the modelling: entities, relationships, one-to-many with pointers, and the ER diagram you draw before you create a second table — Back4App will happily let you build the wrong schema fast.
Exercise
1h soloReplication — set up your own Parse app in your personal repo, following the lecture steps, with a TA in the room.
1h projectNo group code this week. The team hour goes to the user study — interviews run, notes compared, themes starting to show.

Week 05
Sep 24
MirceaLecture · Backend II
Authentication, authorization, and data modeling
Two words that sound alike and mean different things, which is why they are one lecture. Authentication first — Parse.User, signup, login, and the current user, with the app gated on Parse.User.current() and the conditional rendering from week 2, because the router is still two weeks away. Then authorization, the group mechanism. A private list is owner-only; a shared list is a team role. Sharing is by email address, and both parties must already have accounts: no invitations, no pending states, no half-members. The constraint is deliberate — it keeps the model small enough to hold in your head and defend. This is also the collection layer: items point to a List, sharing lives at the list level, and the entity-relationship model grows a join worth drawing.
Exercise
1h soloAdd signup and login to your own app; set an ACL on an object; create and assign a role.
1h projectStill no group code. The user study is in, so now decide what you are building: turn your tasks into an ER diagram for your own domain, and a first list of features.

Week 06
Oct 1
MirceaLecture · Routing + deploy
Routing, pages, and going live

Opens with ten minutes of feedback on the task lists handed in nine days ago — what worked, what was a quote rather than a theme, what will not survive contact with a screen. You have until next Thursday to act on it; the wireframing lecture assumes you have.

Then the rest of week 5, which ran out of time: your questions from re-reading the notes, and sharing a list with a friend — finding them, and what their ACLs and their lists query have to say. Then routing: you have been building a single-page app, which is exactly why it needs client-side routing — pages, and the login gate you wrote in week 5 upgraded from a conditional into a protected route with a URL you can link to.

And then it goes public on GitHub Pages, today, in the room — and immediately 404s when you refresh a route, because a static host knows nothing about client-side routing. Good: that quirk is not a footnote, it is the clearest possible demonstration of what routing actually does, and you only believe it once it has bitten you. Fix it, open the URL on your phone, and leave. Everything after this week is improving something real people can already reach.

Exercise
1h soloAdd a route with a URL parameter; deploy one page and make refresh work.
1h projectThe team's app begins, from an empty repo. Create it in a free GitHub organisation for your team, with all four of you as owners, and build it up together: Vite, then your backend against the ER diagram you drew last week, then routing and pages, then deploy it publicly. Get the URL onto everyone's phone. You are not starting from nothing — each of you has a working Parse app in your own repo from weeks 4 and 5, and that is what you copy the wiring from.

Week 07
Oct 8
KonstantinaLecture · Design IIMircea away
Screens, and judging them: wireframing & usability

You arrive with tasks that have been through a round of feedback and a week of fixing. This is where they become screens — requirements, user flows, and wireframes for what your population actually needs.

Then the other half, because a sketch is worth little until somebody judges it: usability as a quality you can name — learnability, efficiency, memorability, errors, satisfaction — and Nielsen's heuristics as the rough rules for spotting where a screen fails. Then how to run a think-aloud that tells you something.

Sketch rough and sketch fast: cheap to test a crude screen, expensive to test a polished one. That is an argument about fidelity, not tooling — paper is fine, and so is Figma kept deliberately crude: grey boxes, real words, no colour and no type choices. Lea runs a short Figma clinic in the exercise slot for anyone who wants it. Colour and type arrive in week 9; spending them now just makes the thing you are testing harder to change. Accessibility enters here as a design constraint, not a retrofit — and so does the phone. Sketch the narrow screen first — the design is mobile-first, for the whole course. Not breakpoints and flexbox, which come later; just the discipline of deciding what survives when there is one column and a thumb. A layout that works at 375px widens easily. One drawn at 1400px has to be thrown away, and by then it has been tested and everybody is fond of it. You have three weeks and a break to draw, test and revise.

Week 08
Oct 22
KonstantinaLecture · Collaboration + code organisationMircea away
Git-flow, and pulling out the service layer

Group work has properly kicked off — several people pushing to one repo — so this is where collaboration with git-flow earns its keep.

Then the reckoning. Three weeks ago routing multiplied your screens; every one of them has been calling Parse directly ever since, and by now the same query is scattered through six components. Pulling it into a service layer is not a rule handed down — it is relief from a pain you have actually been living with. That is also the first taste of the course's core skill: judging a change against a short checklist of what good code looks like — small components, state where it belongs, clear names, no needless dependencies.

Week 09
Oct 29
KonstantinaLecture · Design III
Making it look right: visual design & accessibility

Opens with feedback on the wireframes: across all groups, out loud, in ten minutes. Then the layer you deliberately did not spend in week 6 — colour, typography, spacing, hierarchy: the principles that separate an app which merely works from one you would keep on your phone. And accessibility as the half you can check: contrast is a visual-design decision and a legal requirement at the same time, and keyboard order, semantics and labels are inspectable in a way that taste is not. The screens were drawn narrow in week 6, so this is widening a design that already works rather than rescuing one that does not — responsiveness lands here if there is time, and in week 12 if there is not. MUI is the vehicle — a design system hands you a type scale, a palette and spacing that already work together, which is the strongest possible argument for use a design system, don't build one, and the point where packages become a judgment. It is also where the AI trap bites hardest: it will hand you a component that looks right and cannot be operated by keyboard.

And one rule starts here and does not stop: no inline styles from this week on. It is not a matter of taste, it is the cheapest possible proxy for your design decisions live somewhere with a name. A colour typed into a component is a decision nobody else can find, reuse or change — the same colour in /design is a system. If you cannot point at the file where a spacing value is defined, you do not have a visual language, you have forty opinions. It joins the review checklist from week 8, and it is trivially checkable, which is the whole reason it is a rule and not advice.

Exercise
1h soloRebuild one screen with MUI in your own repo — the type scale, the palette and the spacing you get for free, and what you gave up to get them.
1h projectAudit the team's app together — keyboard-only pass, contrast, semantics, labels. Write down every failure. Then, if the hour allows, start the responsive pass.

Week 10
Nov 5
MirceaLecture · Code organisation II
Where the state goes: extraction and lifting

The check-in week, so the lecture is a refactor of code you already have rather than a mechanism you have never seen — the exercise slot is spent talking about your own app, which is the wrong place to meet a new API and the right place to meet a new standard.

Since week 8 the review checklist has said state where it belongs without anything ever saying where that is. This is where. Extracting components first, because extraction is what creates the problem: split one screen into three and two of them need to agree about state that now belongs to neither, which is lifting state up. Then useRef, for the two or three things state cannot do. The worked example is the one that bites in week 12 — stopping a task in one list when another starts in a different one.

Week 11
Nov 12
MirceaLecture · Backend III
Talking to the backend well

One subject in three moves, all of it about the wire between your app and Parse. Do less over it: fewer round trips, fetch what you will actually use. Then move work across it, into cloud functions, where it belongs server-side. Then stop asking altogether — live queries, push instead of poll, and the shared list that updates itself while somebody else is typing into it. Two people on one task is where multi-user reality lands on an app you have been using for weeks, and it sets up the collision week 12 has to resolve: if two people track time on the same task, whose time is it?

Examples stay in JavaScript. TypeScript is permitted if a whole group agrees and already has the experience — never as a second track.

Exercise

1h projectMove one operation server-side; put live sync on a shared list.

Week 12
Nov 19
KonstantinaLecture · Feature depthMircea away
Time-tracking, and the idea of context
Opens with feedback on the accessibility audits and visual passes handed in nine days ago. Then: a simple feature that blooms. You cannot run two timers at once, so starting one must stop another — which means the app has to know what is active. That is a context spanning every list, and it is the first thing in the course that is genuinely awkward to hold in your head. Since Parse ACLs are object-level and not field-level, private timing splits into its own table. This is where AI stops being much help, which is rather the point.

How the pieces fit

The exercise slot

1h solo, then 1h project — from week 3 onward. Weeks 1 and 2 are two hours of your own work, because there are no teams yet. Solo drills are required but ungraded — an existence check, not a grading anvil — and they pile up into a personal portfolio that is your exam prep. On the design weeks (3, 7 and 9) the solo hour drills that week's own skill; a couple of times in the back half it swaps "build X" for "review this AI-generated PR on your repo and write three comments you'd defend."

Two repos, two jobs

A shared reference to-do, git-tagged per lecture, is the canonical good code, and it is for reading rather than for starting from. Teams build their own repo from empty in week 6. They have the wiring already — each member set up a Parse app alone in weeks 4 and 5 — and their data model is the ER diagram they argued from their own tasks, so what a copy of the reference would give them is a to-do list they would then have to unpick. Starting empty is also what makes the user study decide the app rather than decorate it — after the user study has said what they are building, and after every member has stood up a backend alone. A personal exercise repo — one folder per week, week-01/ through week-14/, public — holds the solo drills, checked at a glance rather than by pull request. Both URLs are collected in week 1 and week 6, which is what makes checking at a glance possible at all.

The project constraint

Lean required core: owner → lists → items, sharing at the list level. Everything else is an optional feature menu — project grouping, time-tracking with context, two people on one task — that teams pick from and defend. One population, one twist, fully built.

Feedback without pull requests

No weekly PR reviews; they never scaled at this size. What replaced them works on six group artefacts rather than twenty-five individual ones, and it is spoken rather than written: ten minutes at the start of a lecture, across all groups at once, so everybody hears what everybody else got wrong. Around it: dogfooding tells you continuously whether the thing works, AI is your always-on first-pass code reviewer, and two sit-down conversations per group land in weeks 7 and 10.

A pulse, every week

The last two minutes of every lecture: an anonymous single-box form, the same link every week, one question. Read before the next lecture and reported back at the start of it — that second half is what makes students keep filling it in. Fourteen cheap readings beat one end-of-term survey you can no longer act on.

Assessment

70% individual exam, 30% group project, with a hard floor: bomb the individual and you fail, however strong the group. The project is your exam curriculum — if you used it, you understand it.

Pre-course

**JavaScript, the Language is the one module required before week 1, with Scrimba's free tier as the interactive companion (Learn JavaScript, 9.4h, MDN-built; Learn HTML & CSS 5.7h and Learn React 15.1h as bonuses). A Node/npm setup step** runs pre-course. The remaining TopUps arrive on the card of the week they serve.
